source.title: Alpamayo-R1: Bridging Reasoning and Action Prediction for Generalizable Autonomous Driving in the Long Tail
source.authors: Nvidia Yan Wang; Wen-Jie Luo; Jun-Jie Bai; Yu-Long Cao; Tong Che; Ke Chen; Yu-Xiao Chen; Jenna Diamond; Yifan Ding; Wen-Hao Ding; Liang Feng; Greg Heinrich; Jack Huang; Peter Karkus; Bo-Yi Li; Pin-Zu Li; Tsung-Yi Lin; Dong-Run Liu; Ming-Yu Liu; Langechuan Liu; Zhi-Jian Liu; Jason Lu; Yu Mao; Pavlo Molchanov; Lindsey Pavao; Zheng-Hao Peng; Michael Ranzinger; E. Schmerling; Shida Shen; Yun-Fei Shi; Sarah Tariq; Ran Tian; Tilman Wekel; Xinshuo Weng; Tianjun Xiao; Eric Yang; Xiao-Dong Yang; Yu-Rong You; Xiao-Hui Zeng; Wenyuan Zhang; B. Ivanovic; Marco Pavone

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests downstream driving-performance scaling (V6) using trajectory-prediction metrics rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. for the general statement that performance improves with compute and data, but it does not measure language-model pretraining loss, fit power laws to loss, test extrapolation, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Rows below cover its own driving-performance results across model size and training-data size, which bear on V6.
record.test_reason: This is a driving vision-language-action paper, not a language-model scaling study. Its own ablations vary VLM backbone size (0.5B/3B/7B; 0.5B vs 10B) and driving-data size, and report downstream trajectory error (minADE6). That gives a new-setting result on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6). It fits no power law, makes no prediction and never relates performance to pretraining loss, so only the direction of the V6 effect is tested, not its predictability. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the main conclusion is that CoC reasoning supervision plus RL post-training improves driving, especially in challenging long-tail cases. Scaling backbone size and data is a secondary finding: both 'are effective dimensions for improving driving performance'.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales autonomous-driving models and datasets and measures trajectory-prediction error, not held-out language-model cross-entropy across parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that early stopping changes the 100k-data result (1.111m without early stopping; 1.016m with early stopping).
record.problems: The scaling evidence concerns driving-task minADE rather than language-model loss. It uses a limited set of model and data scales and reports no fitted scaling exponents or out-of-range predictions. Numerical values for the model-size ablation are not stated in prose apart from the reported 11% reduction for 7B versus 0.5B.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 13 includes additional data-scale settings, but the text does not give their individual metric values, and the plotted values cannot be confidently assigned to each stated training-data amount. Figure 12's plotted minADE values are likewise not transcribed as prose values; the 0.5B reference and 3B point are retained as figure-only rows.

untested.parts: Predictability: there is no fitted scaling relation, no extrapolation, and no relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss. There are only 2–3 model sizes and several data sizes.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit in the driving or multimodal regime, though data and compute sweeps exist.

missing.what: Table 6 0.5B vs 3B for the base and trajectory-only models: 6.4s 0.996→0.977 and 0.971→0.976; 3s 0.284→0.291 and 0.282→0.293 (no gain or reversal with scale)
Closed-loop scaling, 0.5B vs 10B: close encounter 9%→4%, off-road 19%→16%, AlpaSim score 0.35→0.72
Figure 13 minADE6 against FLOPs for 3.5%, 7.1%, 17.9% and 100% clips (1.00, 0.94, 0.89, 0.81), which conflicts with the prose values

record.verdict_notes: The record's limits_scope label for the missing predictive fit is wrong: that is an untested part, not a qualification. The study's scale comparisons are confounded by changes in architecture and backbone, and training budgets were reduced for the size ablation. It is a weak, direction-only test of V6 in a driving VLA setting.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit or prediction of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison of parameter and token allocations.
The vision-encoder ablation does not test effects of language-model depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of whether a power-law loss form holds across modalities or training regimes.

Tests driving trajectory metrics across selected model and data scales, not a general range of downstream tasks or downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; it does not fit a predictive scaling relation.
No comparison of loss exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, and no analysis of loss-curve bending.

rows.subject: 0.5B model (DINOv2 vision encoder and Qwen2.5-0.5B language model)
rows.stage_stated: Trained on identical data with a reduced training budget for the model-size ablation
rows.note: The text identifies this as the 0.5B reference and states its value as 0.5B baseline, but does not give the minADE6 number in prose.
rows.check: This is the 0.5B reference point and its value is only in Figure 12. It is a comparator, not a result. The 0.5B model also uses a DINOv2 encoder rather than the Qwen2.5-VL encoder, so encoder and size are confounded.

rows.subject: 3B model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B)
rows.stage_stated: Trained on identical data with a reduced training budget for the model-size ablation
rows.note: The text reports consistent improvement as model size increases; the plotted value is not given in prose.
rows.check: Figure 12 text shows '6.7%' for this point, likely the 3B reduction versus 0.5B; the value can be recorded as about 6.7%. The size comparison is confounded with a vision-encoder change (DINOv2 for 0.5B vs Qwen2.5-VL ViT).

rows.subject: 7B model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B)
rows.stage_stated: Trained on identical data with a reduced training budget for the model-size ablation
rows.baseline: 0.5B model; minADE6 value not stated in prose
rows.value: 11% reduction in minADE6 compared to the 0.5B baseline
rows.note: The paper attributes the improvement to increased model capacity.
rows.check: The prose says an 11% reduction and Figure 12 shows 11.5%. The same encoder confound as R2 applies. Training used a reduced budget.

rows.subject: 0.5B model
rows.stage_stated: Trained on 100k video segments; without early stopping
rows.operation_detail: Training-data-size sweep with total training steps held fixed
rows.note: The authors describe this 100k-data model as exhibiting clear overfitting.
rows.check: This is a baseline for the data sweep, not a result. It shows overfitting at 100k segments.

rows.subject: 0.5B model
rows.stage_stated: Trained on 100k video segments; with early stopping
rows.operation_detail: Training-data-size sweep with total training steps held fixed
rows.note: The authors describe this 100k-data model as exhibiting clear overfitting.
rows.check: This is a baseline for the data sweep, not a result. It is the early-stopping variant of the 100k model.

rows.subject: 0.5B model
rows.stage_stated: Trained on 500k video segments; total training steps held fixed across experiments
rows.note: The text also reports the 100k model with early stopping at 1.016m.
rows.check: The baseline is the overfit 100k model without early stopping. Against the early-stopped 100k model (1.016m) the gain is smaller. Figure 13 plots different numbers (1.00, 0.94, 0.89, 0.81 by % clips against FLOPs) that do not match the prose.

rows.subject: 0.5B model
rows.stage_stated: Trained on 2M video segments; total training steps held fixed across experiments
rows.note: The text reports this as the best performance in the data-scale sweep.
rows.check: The gain from 500k to 2M is only 0.880 to 0.874m, nearly flat for 4x data. The conflict between Figure 13 and the prose is unresolved.

rows.subject: AR1-3B (+ Ft. w/ CoC & Traj.)
rows.operation_detail: Comparison of AR1 model sizes on held-out CoC data
rows.note: The paper describes the 3B result as further improvement with increased model capacity.
rows.check: This holds for the CoC-fine-tuned variant only. Other rows of Table 6 show no gain or a slight reversal from 0.5B to 3B; these are not recorded.

rows.subject: Alpamayo-R1-10B
rows.size_stated: 10B VLM backbone; 2B parameter diffusion-based trajectory decoder
rows.operation_detail: Comparison of released model sizes on the public driving benchmark
rows.note: The paper reports this as a 7.0% improvement over Alpamayo-R1-0.5B.
rows.check: The 10B model differs from the 0.5B model in backbone (Cosmos-Reason) and adds a 2B decoder, so it is not a clean size comparison.

relationships.condition: CoC-fine-tuned and released AR1 models, and the 0.5B data sweep, on minADE6 at 6.4s
relationships.reason: Larger backbones and more driving data give lower minADE6 (R2, R3, R8, R9, R6, R7). Comparisons are confounded by encoder or backbone changes, and the data gains flatten from 500k to 2M.
relationships.display_finding: Larger backbones and more driving data reduce minADE6, although encoder or backbone changes confound comparisons and data gains flatten between 500,000 and 2 million examples.

relationships.condition: Non-CoC variants in Table 6 and the 3s horizon
relationships.reason: From the text (Table 6, not in the rows): at 6.4s the trajectory-only fine-tune is 0.976 at 3B vs 0.971 at 0.5B. At 3s, the base and trajectory-only 3B models are worse than 0.5B. The scale gain depends on the fine-tuning recipe and the horizon.
relationships.display_finding: At 6.4 seconds, trajectory-only scores were 0.976 for 3B versus 0.971 for 0.5B, while at three seconds the 3B base and trajectory-only models performed worse.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
